Hi Olivia,

Thanks again for taking the time to evaluate Redwood for Verdant's dedicated/private deployment needs. Attached is our latest compartmentalization topology (compartmentalization-diagram-v3.pdf) and an initial procurement checklist that maps network-level controls to SOC 2 / SIG / CAIQ items.

High-level notes to focus your review on:
- Airlock gateways: dedicated edge-terminating appliances per-customer (logical airlocks) that do TLS termination + WAF rules; used only for inbound control-plane and admin flows.
- Control plane overlay: our control plane runs in a customer-isolated VPC with an encrypted management channel (mTLS) to the service plane; control-plane endpoints are never publicly routable.
- Tenant fences: GPU pools are labeled and pinned by tenant; scheduling enforces tenancy at the allocation layer and we use sidecar sandboxing for process-level isolation on shared nodes.
- Egress guards: egress is forced through customer-configurable NAT + egress proxies (with allowlist). DNS requests are filtered and logged; no direct internet egress from inference containers unless explicitly permitted.
- KMS boundaries: customer-managed keys can be used for model artifacts and KV cache encryption; HSM-backed KMS is supported for Private deployments.

Ask: can you validate whether this topology covers the CAIQ-network/dataflow items Verdant will require for procurement? In particular, we want confirmation on the acceptability of sidecar-based process isolation versus a full air-gapped host hypervisor approach for your auditors.

I attached: compartmentalization-diagram-v3.pdf (annotated), procurement-network-checklist.xlsx (first pass), and the drawio file. If it helps, I'm available for a 45-minute walkthrough; propose Tue 9/22 10:00-10:45 PT or Wed 9/23 14:00-14:45 PT.

1) For the sidecar sandboxing on shared nodes: do you have measurable NVs (noise vectors) or microbenchmarks showing that tenant KV cache and model artifacts cannot be accessed cross-tenant? Our security team usually asks for design + test evidence (process isolation + SELinux/AppArmor profiles or equivalent).

2) Control plane overlay: can you provide the CIDR isolation model you use for the management network and a short description of how route leaks are prevented when Dedicated pools span multiple AZs? In particular, auditors want to see explicit egress filtering on management subnets.

3) For KMS/HSM: can you confirm whether Redwood's Private package supports customer-supplied HSM modules and whether keys are accessible to any host processes (i.e., do keys ever leave the HSM in plaintext for caching)?

Olivia — great questions. Quick answers inline below; I'll bring artifacts and brief demos to the 9/23 call.

1) Sidecar sandboxing / cross-tenant leakage
- Design: workloads use a minimal sidecar process that mediates access to the local KV cache and model artifacts. Sidecar enforces a tenant ID token that is validated by the runtime; requests without the token are dropped.
- Hardening evidence: we can provide a packet of tests we run during onboarding (process isolation smoke tests, mmap/procfs access checks, SELinux policy snippets where applicable). For Private installs we can enable additional host-level hardening (AppArmor/SELinux or gVisor).
- Benchmark note: we have a microbench that proves KV namespace separation (latency and throughput baselines) and fuzz tests for access attempts; I will attach the test-report PDF to the call notes.

2) Control plane overlay + CIDR model
- CIDR pattern: management/control plane ranges are allocated from a distinct RFC1918 block per customer (10.250.0.0/16 by default) and we publish the allocated subranges in the onboarding sheet. Each AZ gets a /24 for control endpoints; route propagation is limited to the management VPC via AWS route tables and explicit prefix lists.
- Route leak prevention: control-plane subnets are isolated via AWS prefix-lists and strict Security Group rules that only permit mTLS to service-plane endpoints. We also deploy host-based iptables rules to block accidental routing between the management and service subnets.
- Egress filtering: yes — all management subnet egress goes through a managed NAT/egress proxy; control-plane nodes cannot reach arbitrary internet hosts.

3) KMS/HSM handling
- Private: supports customer HSMs (PKCS#11) and Redwood's control plane talks to them over an HSM gateway; keys do not leave the HSM in plaintext. We can provide an HSM integration spec for your HSM vendor.
- Hosted: Redwood-managed KMS stores keys wrapped by a root we hold; we never export private key material as plaintext to external systems.

Attachments for the call: a short test-report PDF (KV-separation-test-report.pdf), the updated drawio with CIDR labels (control-plane-overlay.drawio), and the procurement spreadsheet updated with a CAIQ mapping column.

I'll plan to demo the sidecar token validation and show the route table + prefix-list configuration during the walkthrough. 9/23 14:00 PT is on my calendar.

See you then,

Diego Fernandez
